notes.meaning: Bezalel, the chief craftsman chosen by God, began building the sacred ark using durable acacia wood. It was built as a chest about forty-five inches long, twenty-seven inches wide, and twenty-seven inches high, small enough to be carried. Recording these exact details shows that the builders carefully followed the exact pattern God gave on the mountain.

Bezalel covered the wooden chest with pure gold inside and out, and added an ornamental gold border around its top edge. Covering simple wood with pure gold showed the ark's holiness and pointed to how God's heavenly presence meets with humanity. The chest was designed to keep God's law safe and honored at its center.

Bezalel cast four gold rings and fastened them to the four feet of the ark. He also made carrying poles from acacia wood covered in gold and slipped them into the rings. These poles allowed the priests to transport God's holy chest respectfully on their shoulders without ever touching it directly.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition notes that the carrying poles were never to be removed from the rings, remaining in place even after the ark was later set inside Solomon's temple.

notes.meaning: Bezalel crafted the mercy seat, the solid gold lid that rested on top of the ark, measuring forty-five inches long and twenty-seven inches wide. This lid was not wood overlaid with gold, but was made entirely of pure gold. It served as the place where God met his people in mercy, showing that his grace and forgiveness cover human sin.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching explains that the mercy seat foreshadowed Christ, who makes propitiation—reconciliation and peace with God—for our sins, serving as God's throne while the ark acted as his footstool.

notes.meaning: Bezalel hammered two winged heavenly creatures, called cherubim, out of solid gold at both ends of the mercy seat. They were not made separately and attached, but were beaten out of the very same piece of gold as the lid itself. Shaping such detailed figures with a hammer from one solid piece of gold required extraordinary skill given by God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching notes that having two cherubim rather than one showed the multitude of heavenly angels and kept Israel from worshipping them as an idol.

notes.meaning: The cherubim spread their wings upward to overshadow the mercy seat, while their faces turned inward toward each other and down toward the lid. Their posture showed their reverent attention to God's presence and their unity in serving him. Instead of looking down at the law that condemns sinners, they gazed upon the place where God displays his mercy through sacrifice.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching interprets the two cherubim facing one another as a picture showing that the heavenly spirits live in perfect peace and harmony with one another.

notes.meaning: Bezalel built the table for the holy bread of the Presence out of acacia wood, three feet long, eighteen inches wide, and twenty-seven inches high. This table stood in the Holy Place to display bread continually before the Lord. It pictured God as a generous provider who feeds his people and welcomes them to live in fellowship with him.

He overlaid the wooden table with pure gold and fashioned an ornamental gold molding around it. He also added a rim about three inches wide around the edges, with its own gold border. This raised rim kept the loaves of bread and the sacred dishes safely on the table as a boundary of holiness.

Four gold rings were cast and attached to the four corners near the table's legs, close to the protective rim. Bezalel then made carrying poles of acacia wood overlaid with gold and placed them through the rings. These poles allowed the priests to lift and transport the holy table securely whenever Israel moved camp.

All the utensils for the table—including plates for bread, incense dishes, bowls, and pitchers for pouring drink offerings—were made of pure gold. These vessels were used in the ongoing worship and offerings presented before God in the Holy Place. Using pure gold for every cup and plate showed that God deserves the very best and purest in his worship.

Bezalel constructed the lampstand out of one piece of pure hammered gold, including its central stem, base, decorative cups, buds, and flower petals. Unlike the ark and table, the lampstand had no wood underneath, being shaped entirely from precious metal. It provided light in the Holy Place, pointing to the light of God's Word and truth among his people.

Six branches extended outward from the lampstand's central shaft, three on one side and three on the other. Each branch was decorated with three cups shaped like almond blossoms, complete with buds and petals. These detailed plant designs reflected the beauty of God's creation, while almond blossoms specifically symbolized alertness and life.

The main stem of the lampstand had four almond-shaped cups with matching buds and petals. A decorative bud was set beneath each of the three pairs of branches that branched out from the center shaft. Every detail was crafted so that the whole structure formed a single, harmonious tree of light.

The ornamental buds, branches, and central shaft were not made as separate pieces joined together. Instead, the entire lampstand was beaten out of a single lump of pure gold. This unified design highlighted the flawless harmony and beauty of God's sanctuary.

Bezalel made seven oil lamps to sit on the branches, along with gold wick trimmers and trays to maintain them. The whole lampstand and all its tools were hammered out of one talent of pure gold, weighing around seventy-five pounds. The bright, steady light of the seven lamps illuminated the daily work of the priests in the sanctuary.

Bezalel built the incense altar out of acacia wood as a square measuring eighteen inches long, eighteen inches wide, and three feet high. Corner projections shaped like animal horns were crafted out of the same wood as the altar. These horns represented strength and refuge, and they received the blood of atonement once a year on the Day of Atonement.

The top, sides, and horns of the altar were overlaid with pure gold, and finished with a gold molding around the edge. Because it stood inside the tent near God's presence, it was covered in gold rather than bronze. The sweet smoke rising from this golden altar symbolized the prayers of God's people ascending to him.

Two gold rings were fixed beneath the molding on opposite sides to hold the acacia-wood poles overlaid with gold. These poles allowed the altar to be lifted and transported easily as Israel moved through the wilderness. Overlaying even the carrying poles with gold showed the great dignity of the holy worship inside the tent.

Finally, Bezalel prepared the sacred anointing oil and the pure, fragrant incense according to the craft of a skilled perfumer. Although he was primarily a builder and metalworker, God gave him the wisdom and skill to mix these fragrant compounds with exact precision. The sweet incense was burned daily on the golden altar, while the holy oil set apart the tent and priests for God's service.
